Meaning (English): Used to say what something is. Ends in 「이에요」 if the noun has a final consonant, and 「예요」 if it does not.
Watch out: Use 「이에요」 after a final consonant and 「예요」 after a vowel. It is 「친구예요」, not 「친구이에요」.

Meaning (English): Says whether something exists or not. Also used for having something.
Watch out: 「있다」 covers both existing and owning. You also say 「있어요」 for what you have.

Meaning (English): Korean has two number systems: Sino-Korean (prices, dates, minutes) and native Korean (counting items, age, hours).
Form: Sino-Korean: 「일, 이, 삼...」 / Native Korean: 「하나, 둘, 셋...」
Watch out: Before counting units, 「하나, 둘, 셋, 넷」 change to 「한, 두, 세, 네」. Say 「두 잔」, not 「둘 잔」.

Meaning (English): Dates are read using Sino-Korean numbers. Days of the week attach 「요일」 to the day name.
Watch out: June is pronounced 「유월」 (not 「육월」), and October is pronounced 「시월」 (not 「십월」).

Meaning (English): Hours are read in native Korean numbers, while minutes are read in Sino-Korean numbers.
Watch out: Say 「세 시 삼십 분」, not 「삼 시 삼십 분」. 30 minutes can also be called 「반」.

Meaning (English): The most formal speech style. Used in presentations, meetings, news broadcasts, and when meeting someone for the first time.
Form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㅂ니다」 / with final consonant + 「-습니다」
Watch out: Questions end in 「-(스)ㅂ니까?」. Using this style with close friends sounds overly stiff.

Meaning (English): The most common everyday polite style. It sounds polite and soft, making it suitable for almost any daily situation.
Form: After stems ending in 「ㅏ, ㅗ」: 「-아요」 / Other vowels: 「-어요」 / 「하다」 verbs: 「해요」
Watch out: Raise your intonation at the end to make it a question without changing the word form, like 「먹어요?」.

Meaning (English): Used to talk about actions or states that have already ended in the past.
Form: After stems ending in 「ㅏ, ㅗ」: 「-았어요」 / Other vowels: 「-었어요」 / 「하다」 verbs: 「했어요」
Watch out: 「-았/었어요」 is for completed events. If an action or state is still ongoing right now, use 「-고 있어요」.

Meaning (English): Used to talk about future actions or plans that have already been decided.
Form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 거예요」 / with final consonant + 「-을 거예요」
Watch out: Pronounced as [-ㄹ 꺼에요] when spoken, but must always be written as 「거예요」.

Meaning (English): Indicates that an action is currently in progress right now.
Watch out: Use 「-고 계세요」 for honored elders or teachers, as in 「선생님이 기다리고 계세요」.

Meaning (English): Used to emphasize that a past state or event is no longer true today.
Watch out: The key meaning is that the present is different. For simple completed past events, 「-았/었어요」 is enough.

Meaning (English): Words that have their own distinct antonyms instead of taking the negative prefix 「안」.
Watch out: Do not say 「안 알아요」 or 「안 있어요」. Use 「몰라요」 and 「없어요」 instead.

Meaning (English): Expresses simple negative action or your intention not to do something.
Watch out: For compound verbs like 「공부하다」 (Noun + 「하다」), place 「안」 in the middle: 「공부 안 해요」, not 「안 공부해요」.

Meaning (English): Expresses that you want to do something but cannot due to lack of ability or circumstances.
Watch out: 「안」 means choosing not to do something, while 「못」 means being unable to do it. Swapping them changes the meaning.

Meaning (English): Subject marker pointing out who or what performs the action. Often introduces new information.
Form: Noun with final consonant + 「이」 / without final consonant + 「가」
Watch out: While 「저는」 introduces yourself as the topic, 「제가」 specifically highlights you as the person who did the action.

Meaning (English): Topic marker used to introduce what you are talking about or to draw a contrast with something else.
Form: Noun with final consonant + 「은」 / without final consonant + 「는」
Watch out: Particularly natural for contrasting two things, as in 「커피는 좋아하는데 차는 안 좋아해요」.

Meaning (English): Object marker indicating the target of an action.
Form: Noun with final consonant + 「을」 / without final consonant + 「를」
Watch out: Frequently dropped in casual spoken Korean. Saying 「밥 먹었어요?」 sounds more natural.

Meaning (English): Joins two nouns, or says you did something together with someone. All three mean the same and differ only in tone.
Watch out: 「와/과」 suits writing, 「(이)랑」 suits friends. 「하고」 is safe anywhere.

Meaning (English): Possessive marker indicating ownership or belonging.
Watch out: It is much more natural to shorten 「나의」 to 「내」 and 「저의」 to 「제」.

Meaning (English): Indicates the location where something exists or the time when an event occurs.
Watch out: Use 「에」 for static location of existence, and 「에서」 for dynamic action: 「집에 있어요 / 집에서 일해요」.

Meaning (English): Indicates a destination you are heading toward, or marks a unit of measurement/price.
Watch out: The 「에」 in 「학교에 가요」 (direction) and in 「한 개에 천 원」 (unit) share the same spelling but serve different functions.

Meaning (English): Marks where something happens, or where it starts from.
Watch out: For a place where an action happens, use 「에서」, not 「에」: 「카페에서 만나요」.

Meaning (English): Expresses 'from where to where' for locations, and 'from when to when' for time.
Watch out: Use 「에서」 for starting locations and 「부터」 for starting points in time: 「아홉 시부터 여섯 시까지」.

Meaning (English): Marks the person you give something to or say something to.
Watch out: Use 「께」 for someone senior. For a thing rather than a person, use 「에」: 「회사에 연락했어요」.

Meaning (English): Particle meaning 'also' or 'too', indicating addition or inclusion.
Watch out: When 「도」 is attached, particles like 「이/가」, 「은/는」, and 「을/를」 are dropped. Say 「저도」, not 「저는도」.

Meaning (English): Particle meaning 'only' or 'just', indicating exclusivity.
Watch out: 「만」 replaces subject and object markers. It is also commonly used in polite requests like 「잠깐만요」.

Meaning (English): Nothing but that — and it feels like too little.
Watch out: What follows must be negative. 「천 원밖에 있어요」 is wrong.

Meaning (English): Indicates a tool, method, direction, or material used.
Form: Noun without final consonant or ending in 「ㄹ」 + 「로」 / other consonants + 「으로」
Watch out: Nouns ending in 「ㄹ」 take 「로」 without 「으」. Say 「연필로」, not 「연필으로」.

Meaning (English): Particle expressing an option between choices, meaning 'or'.
Form: Noun with final consonant + 「이나」 / without final consonant + 「나」
Watch out: Use 「-거나」 to connect verbs and 「(이)나」 to connect nouns.

Meaning (English): Attached to numbers to express surprise that an amount is more than expected.
Watch out: When an amount is disappointingly small, use 「밖에」 instead. Compare with 「세 시간밖에 못 잤어요」.

Meaning (English): Attached to nouns to indicate an approximation or estimate.
Watch out: Placing 「한」 before the noun makes it sound even more natural: 「한 시간쯤」.

Meaning (English): Compares something to what it resembles.
Watch out: 「같이」 also means 'together', so use 「처럼」 where that could confuse.

Meaning (English): Compares two things and says which one is more.
Watch out: 「보다」 attaches to what you compare against. 「어제보다 춥다」 means today is colder.

Meaning (English): Every one without exception, or repeating at that interval.
Watch out: 「매일」 is one word and 「날마다」 is a particle. Both are natural.

Meaning (English): Connects two actions or states side by side, or lists sequential actions.
Watch out: The subjects in both clauses can be different, as in 「저는 자고 동생은 공부했어요」.

Meaning (English): One or the other — a choice between two actions.
Watch out: To join nouns instead, use 「(이)나」: 「커피나 차」.

Meaning (English): The first half and the second half go against each other.
Watch out: The plainest way to contrast two things. It never sounds out of place.

Meaning (English): Smoothly connects contrasting clauses. It sounds far more natural in conversation than 「-지만」.
Watch out: While 「-지만」 creates a sharp contrast, 「-는데」 introduces a gentle contrast and is much more common in speech.

Meaning (English): Before that — you do this first.
Watch out: A verb always needs 「-기」: 「먹기 전에」, not 「먹 전에」.

Meaning (English): After that thing has finished.
Form: N 후에 · V + (으)ㄴ 후에 · same meaning: -(으)ㄴ 다음에
Watch out: A verb takes the past form 「-(으)ㄴ」: 「먹은 후에」, not 「먹는 후에」.

Meaning (English): You finish the first thing completely, then do the next.
Watch out: Makes the finishing clearer than plain 「-고」 does.

Meaning (English): Expresses that the first action is completed and directly connected to the following action.
Watch out: 「-고」 merely lists actions, while 「-아/어서」 links them sequentially. 「친구를 만나고 밥을 먹었어요」 implies eating separately.

Meaning (English): At that time, or around when that happens.
Form: N 때 · A/V + (으)ㄹ 때 · past -았/었을 때
Watch out: After a noun it attaches directly, with no 「-을」: 「방학 때」.

Meaning (English): Doing two things at the same time.
Form: -면서 after a vowel · -으면서 after a consonant
Watch out: Both halves need the same subject. 「제가 자면서 동생이 공부해요」 is wrong.

Meaning (English): Indicates that someone is in the middle of doing an action right now.
Watch out: Similar in meaning to 「-고 있다」, but 「-는 중」 sounds slightly more formal or stiff.

Meaning (English): The next thing happens the instant the first one ends.
Watch out: For almost no gap in time — much faster than 「-고 나서」.

Meaning (English): Throughout that stretch of time.
Watch out: With 「-는 동안」 the two subjects may differ: 「제가 자는 동안 비가 왔어요」.

Meaning (English): Used to state how much time has passed since doing an action.
Watch out: Followed by verbs like 「되다, 지나다, 넘다」. Distinct from the clause connector 「-는지」 (checking information).
Example (Korean): 한국에 온 지 일 년 됐어요.

Meaning (English): Says whether you can or cannot do something. Covers both ability and possibility.
Form: -ㄹ 수 after a vowel · -을 수 after a consonant
Watch out: Softer than 「못」. To turn something down, 「갈 수 없어요」 is gentler than 「못 가요」.
Example (Korean): 저는 한국어를 조금 할 수 있어요.

Meaning (English): Expresses knowing or not knowing how to do something as a learned skill.
Form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 줄」 / with final consonant + 「-을 줄」 + 「알다/모르다」
Watch out: Used for learned skills. Being unable to do something due to external circumstances requires 「-(으)ㄹ 수 없다」.

Meaning (English): Asks or tells someone to do something, politely. It also raises the listener.
Form: -세요 after a vowel · -으세요 after a consonant
Watch out: A few verbs change entirely: 「먹다」 becomes 「드세요」, 「자다」 becomes 「주무세요」.

Meaning (English): A polite way to tell or ask someone not to do something.
Watch out: Cannot attach to adjectives. Phrases like 「예쁘지 마세요」 are incorrect.

Meaning (English): Expresses necessity or obligation, meaning one must do something.
Watch out: 「되다」 is more common in spoken Korean, while 「하다」 fits written Korean better. Their meanings are identical.

Meaning (English): Used to give permission, meaning it is okay to do something.
Watch out: Very frequently used when asking for permission. 「-아/어도 괜찮아요」 carries the same meaning.

Meaning (English): Used to prohibit an action, stating that one must not do it.
Form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-면」 / with final consonant + 「-으면」 + 「안 되다」
Watch out: While 「-지 마세요」 directly asks someone to stop, this form explains a prohibition or rule.

Meaning (English): Means that it is completely fine not to do something.
Form: Verb stem + 「-지 않아도 되다」 · Same meaning as 「안」 + Verb stem + 「-아/어도 되다」
Watch out: This is the opposite of 「-아/어야 되다」. 「안 와도 돼요」 is shorter and more common.

Meaning (English): Expresses that you want to do something.
Form: Verb stem + 「-고 싶다」 · For someone else's desire: 「-고 싶어하다」
Watch out: Use 「-고 싶어해요」 for other people's desires: 「동생이 가고 싶어해요」.

Meaning (English): Expresses a wish for something to happen when it has not happened yet.
Watch out: Although the form looks past tense, it refers to a future wish. 「-면 좋겠다」 carries the same meaning.

Meaning (English): States that something happened because of this reason. It is the most basic way to express cause.
Watch out: It cannot be followed by commands or suggestions. You cannot say 「추워서 창문을 닫으세요」; use 「추우니까」 instead.

Meaning (English): Gives a reason. Unlike 「-아/어서」, a request or a suggestion can follow.
Form: -니까 after a vowel · -으니까 after a consonant
Watch out: For thanks or apologies use 「-아/어서」: 「와 주셔서 감사합니다」.

Meaning (English): Names the cause plainly. Common in writing.
Watch out: No command can follow. Note that 「저 때문에」 means 'my fault', so use it carefully.

Meaning (English): Asks someone to do something for you. The second form is more polite.
Watch out: Adding 「좀」 makes it much softer. 「-아/어 주시겠어요?」 is the most polite form.

Meaning (English): Offers to do something for someone, or asks if they want you to do it.
Watch out: Use 「-아/어 드릴게요」 when offering help to someone you honor: 「제가 도와 드릴게요」.

Meaning (English): Means trying something out. It is also often used when making suggestions.
Watch out: 「-아/어 봤어요」 expresses past experience, while 「-아/어 보세요」 is a suggestion to try something.

Meaning (English): Expresses past experience by stating whether something has happened or not.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-ㄴ 적이」 · With final consonant: 「-은 적이」
Watch out: This fits notable life experiences rather than routine, recent past events. Saying 「어제 밥 먹은 적이 있어요」 sounds awkward.

Meaning (English): Suggests doing something together by asking the listener's thought.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-ㄹ까요」 · With final consonant: 「-을까요」
Watch out: You can answer with 「좋아요」, 「그래요」, or 「-(으)ㅂ시다」.

Meaning (English): Asks if the listener would like you to do something.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-ㄹ까요」 · With final consonant: 「-을까요」
Watch out: Usage ① means 'Shall we do it together?', while usage ② means 'Shall I do it?'. Adding 「제가」 clarifies the meaning.

Meaning (English): Suggests doing something together. It suits formal situations.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-ㅂ시다」 · With final consonant: 「-읍시다」
Watch out: Do not use this with elders or superiors. 「-(으)시겠어요?」 or 「-(으)ㄹ까요?」 is safer.

Meaning (English): Asks someone's preference very politely. It is frequently used when serving guests.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-시겠어요」 · With final consonant: 「-으시겠어요」
Watch out: This is the most polite way to make an inquiry or offer, ideal for addressing customers in stores or offices.

Meaning (English): Casually asks what the listener wants to do among close acquaintances.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-ㄹ래요」 · With final consonant: 「-을래요」
Watch out: Because it has a casual tone, it is not suitable for elders, superiors, or formal settings.

Meaning (English): Declares your clear intention to do something.
Watch out: Used when stating your firm intention in formal settings: 「알겠습니다」, 「하겠습니다」.

Meaning (English): Tells the listener you will do something as if making a promise.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-ㄹ게요」 · With final consonant: 「-을게요」
Watch out: The subject is always 'I'. You cannot say 「친구가 올게요」; say 「올 거예요」 instead.

Meaning (English): Casually states your own choice or intention to do something.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-ㄹ래요」 · With final consonant: 「-을래요」
Watch out: Because it strongly emphasizes personal intention, it is better to use 「-(으)ㄹ게요」 in front of elders or superiors.

Meaning (English): Provides relevant background context before bringing up the main point. Used very often in Korean conversation.
Watch out: It sounds especially natural when bringing up a request: 「죄송한데 길 좀 여쭤볼게요」.

Meaning (English): Means discovering a fact after trying or experiencing something.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-니까」 · With final consonant: 「-으니까」
Watch out: It shares the same form as 「-(으)니까」 for reasons. If a newly discovered fact follows, it expresses discovery.

Meaning (English): States that you go or come in order to do something.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-러」 · With final consonant: 「-으러」 + 「가다 / 오다 / 다니다」
Watch out: Only movement verbs like 'go' and 'come' can follow. You cannot say 「먹으러 공부해요」.

Meaning (English): You do something with that intention.
Form: -려고 after a vowel · -으려고 after a consonant
Watch out: No command or suggestion can follow. Use 「-(으)려면」 or 「-도록」 for that.

Meaning (English): Means you intend to do something, or that something is about to happen.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-려고」 · With final consonant: 「-으려고」 + 「하다」
Watch out: It feels less definite than 「-(으)ㄹ 거예요」, making it ideal when you are still in the planning stage.

Meaning (English): Says what the purpose is. It suits writing.
Form: N + 을/를 위해서 · V + 기 위해서
Watch out: Stiffer than 「-(으)려고」, which sounds more natural when speaking.

Meaning (English): Means deciding to do something.
Watch out: Used both for decisions made on your own and for promises made with others.

Meaning (English): Means 'if' or 'when' something happens. Widely used for conditions and suppositions.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-면」 · With final consonant: 「-으면」
Watch out: This is the most widely used conditional expression. Adding 「만약」 in front strengthens the sense of hypothetical condition.

Meaning (English): If you intend to do that — and what follows is what it takes.
Form: -려면 after a vowel · -으려면 after a consonant
Watch out: Unlike 「-(으)려고」, a command or a suggestion can follow.

Meaning (English): Means that even in such a situation, the outcome remains unchanged.
Form: Adjective/Verb stem + 「-아도 / -어도」 · Often used with 「아무리」 in front
Watch out: If 「-(으)면」 sets a condition, 「-아/어도」 means doing something regardless of that condition.

Meaning (English): Makes an immediate guess based on what you see, hear, or feel right now.
Watch out: An immediate guess based on what you see. It is frequently used to show empathy, like 「힘들겠어요」 or 「피곤하겠어요」.

Meaning (English): Expresses a guess that something is likely the case.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-ㄹ 거예요」 · With final consonant: 「-을 거예요」
Watch out: It has the same form as the future plan in ①. If the subject is another person, it is usually a conjecture.

Meaning (English): Wonders together whether something might happen.
Form: Without final consonant: 「-ㄹ까요」 · With final consonant: 「-을까요」
Watch out: Unlike the suggestion form of 「-(으)ㄹ까요?」, this is closer to thinking out loud and does not require an answer.

Meaning (English): Softly expresses that something seems to be the case. Frequently used to avoid sounding overly direct.
Form: Past: 「-(으)ㄴ」 · Present verb: 「-는」 / Adjective: 「-(으)ㄴ」 · Future: 「-(으)ㄹ 것 같다」
Watch out: Also used to express personal thoughts softly. 「좋은 것 같아요」 sounds much more tentative and polite than 「좋아요」.

Meaning (English): Changes verbs and adjectives into forms that attach in front of nouns to modify them.
Watch out: The present-tense modifier for adjectives is 「-(으)ㄴ」. It is 「예쁜 옷」, not 「예쁘는 옷」.

Meaning (English): Turns verbs and adjectives into nouns.
Watch out: Many words have become fixed vocabulary with this ending, such as 「읽기, 쓰기, 듣기, 말하기」.

Meaning (English): Turns adjectives into adverbs to describe how an action is performed.
Watch out: Frequently used in common greetings, like 「맛있게 드세요」 and 「재미있게 보내세요」.

Meaning (English): Used to describe another person's emotions observed from the outside.
Watch out: Use simple adjectives for your own feelings, but use 「-아/어하다」 for others' feelings: 「저는 좋아요 / 동생은 좋아해요」.

Meaning (English): Indicates the ongoing state of wearing clothing, accessories, or footwear.
Watch out: 「지금 옷을 입고 있어요」 can mean both 'in the process of putting clothes on' and 'currently wearing clothes'.

Meaning (English): Indicates that a state continues after an action has finished.
Watch out: It does not attach to verbs that take an object. You cannot say 「밥을 먹어 있어요」.

Meaning (English): Indicates a gradual change of state.
Watch out: Attaches to adjectives to indicate a change of state: 「예뻐지다」, 「좋아지다」.

Meaning (English): Means that something ended up happening regardless of your own intention.
Watch out: It implies that the outcome was not entirely your own decision, and is also used to deliver news carefully.

Meaning (English): Connects an uncertain clause within a sentence.
Watch out: This is different from 「-(으)ㄴ 지」 (time elapsed), which is written with a space.

Meaning (English): Expresses how much time or money it takes to do something.
Watch out: Use 「걸리다」 for time and 「들다」 for money. Leave a space before 「데」.
Example (Korean): 여기까지 오는 데 한 시간 걸렸어요.

Meaning (English): Used to ask for confirmation about something you already know. Shortened to 「-죠?」 in speech.
Watch out: Used to seek agreement or confirm facts, not to ask for brand-new information.

Meaning (English): Expresses a realization or exclamation upon learning something you did not know before.
Watch out: Used for newly discovered facts. It sounds unnatural for things you already knew.

Meaning (English): Expresses spontaneous admiration or reaction to what you are currently seeing or feeling directly.
Watch out: While 「-군요」 marks realization, 「-네요」 shares an immediate impression. It is much more common in speech.

Meaning (English): Used to ask questions softly. It sounds more cautious and gentle than 「-아/어요?」.
Watch out: Well suited for first meetings or formal inquiries.

Meaning (English): Leaves the sentence open to create a lingering nuance. Used to decline softly or express mild surprise.
Watch out: Sounds gentle because it avoids blunt conclusions. Especially common when declining something.

Meaning (English): Quotes someone's exact words directly as they were spoken.
Watch out: Keep the words inside the quotation marks exactly as they were spoken without changing them.

Meaning (English): Paraphrases and reports what you heard in your own words.
Watch out: The form splits into four types based on sentence kind. Telling these four apart is key.

Meaning (English): Shortened forms of indirect quotations used in spoken Korean.
Watch out: Shortened forms are far more natural in speech. Use full forms in formal writing.

Meaning (English): When stems ending in 「ㅡ」 meet 「-아/어」, the vowel 「ㅡ」 drops.
Watch out: Look at the vowel in the preceding syllable to choose between 「아」 and 「어」. 「바쁘다」 has 「ㅏ」, so it becomes 「바빠요」.

Meaning (English): The final consonant 「ㄹ」 drops before 「ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ」.
Watch out: 「ㄹ」 also drops before 「-는」, as in 「사는 곳」 and 「만드는 법」.

Meaning (English): When the final consonant 「ㅂ」 meets a vowel, it changes to 「우」.
Watch out: Only 「돕다」 and 「곱다」 change to 「오」 instead of 「우」: 「도와요」, 「고와요」.

Meaning (English): When the final consonant 「ㄷ」 meets a vowel, it changes to 「ㄹ」.
Watch out: Verbs like 「받다」, 「닫다」, and 「믿다」 do not change: 「받아요」, 「닫아요」.

Meaning (English): When stems ending in 「르」 meet 「-아/어」, it changes into a double 「ㄹ」 (「ㄹㄹ」).
Watch out: 「따르다」 and 「들르다」 follow regular 「ㅡ」 irregular rules: 「따라요」, 「들러요」.

Meaning (English): When the final consonant 「ㅅ」 meets a vowel, it drops.
Watch out: Verbs like 「웃다」, 「씻다」, and 「벗다」 do not change: 「웃어요」, 「씻어요」.

Meaning (English): For adjectives with a final consonant 「ㅎ」, the 「ㅎ」 drops and the vowel changes.
Watch out: Applies only to adjectives. Verbs like 「좋다」 and 「넣다」 do not change: 「좋아요」, 「넣어요」.

Meaning (English): Expresses an outward visual impression, meaning something looks or appears a certain way.
Watch out: Attaches to adjectives. Distinct from 「-아/어 보다」 (to try doing something), which attaches to verbs.

Meaning (English): Expresses an inference based on what you observe. Used about other people or external situations.
Form: Verb stem + 「-는 모양이다」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 모양이다」 / Past tense + 「-(으)ㄴ 모양이다」
Watch out: Do not use for your own direct actions or states. Saying 「제가 아픈 모양이에요」 is unnatural.
Example (Korean): 불이 꺼진 걸 보니 아무도 없는 모양이에요.

Meaning (English): Expresses worry or regret while guessing a likely situation.
Form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 텐데」 / with final consonant + 「-을 텐데」
Watch out: Usually followed by a concern or suggestion, as in 「배고플 텐데 이거 드세요」.

Meaning (English): Indicates that the speaker will do something, or presumes a situation, and tells the listener what to do.
Form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 테니까」 / with final consonant + 「-을 테니까」
Watch out: Followed by a command or suggestion. 「-(으)ㄹ 텐데」 expresses worry, while this provides a reason for action.

Meaning (English): Expresses a light guess about something you are not entirely sure of.
Form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ걸요」 / with final consonant + 「-을걸요」
Watch out: Resembles the regret expression 「-(으)ㄹ걸 그랬다」. Pronounce it with a slight upward intonation.

Meaning (English): Expresses that you did not expect something at all. Saying you knew means the opposite.
Form: Past: 「-(으)ㄴ 줄」 / Present: 「-는 줄」 / Future: 「-(으)ㄹ 줄」 + 「알았다」 / 「몰랐다」
Watch out: Distinct from ability in 「-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다」 (knowing how to do). This expresses an assumption.

Meaning (English): Expresses that there is a possibility that something might happen.
Form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ지도」 / with final consonant + 「-을지도」 + 「모르다」
Watch out: Gives a feeling of a roughly fifty-fifty chance. Frequently used when suggesting to pack an umbrella.

Meaning (English): Acknowledges one point first while stepping back to mention another contrasting aspect.
Watch out: First admits the preceding fact before contrasting it. Softer than 「-지만」.

Meaning (English): Contrasts two opposing sides side by side, showing one is this way while the other is the opposite.
Form: Verb stem + 「-는 반면에」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 반면에」
Watch out: Used to compare two subjects side by side. Especially common in written Korean.

Meaning (English): Expresses that something happened despite expectations to the contrary.
Form: Verb stem + 「-는데도」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ데도」 / Past tense + 「-았/었는데도」
Watch out: While 「-아/어도」 is hypothetical, this describes a real, completed fact.

Meaning (English): Written narrative style used in newspapers, novels, diaries, and reports without addressing a specific listener.
Watch out: Sounds like informal speech when spoken aloud. Strictly used in writing.

Meaning (English): Informal, casual speech style used with close friends or younger people.
Watch out: Simply drop 「요」. Do not use with people you just met or with elders.

Meaning (English): Shares a reason that the listener does not know yet.
Watch out: The reason comes at the end of the conversation, unlike 「-(으)니까」 where the cause comes first.

Meaning (English): Reminds the listener of a fact that they already know.
Watch out: If used for something the listener does not know, it sounds argumentative. Use only for shared knowledge.

Meaning (English): Indicates that doing one action prevented another, resulting in a negative outcome.
Watch out: The subject must be the same in both clauses, and past tense is not used before it: say 「하느라고」, not 「했느라고」.

Meaning (English): Indicates that an unexpected event occurred and caused a negative result.
Watch out: Used for sudden situations outside your control. What follows is usually a negative outcome.

Meaning (English): Points out a cause in a blaming tone, stating it was the fault of that event.
Form: Verb stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 탓에」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 탓에」 / Noun + 「탓에」
Watch out: Do not use for positive events. For good results, use 「덕분에」.

Meaning (English): Mentions one of several reasons casually without listing them all.
Watch out: Sounds more natural when paired with 「도」. Used when you choose not to list every single reason.

Meaning (English): You are worried it might turn out that way, so you do something about it first.
Form: -ㄹ까 봐 after a vowel · -을까 봐 after a consonant
Watch out: What follows is what the worry made you do. Only for bad outcomes.

Meaning (English): Repeats what you heard in disbelief to ask for confirmation.
Watch out: Used to ask back in surprise, or to re-confirm when you did not hear clearly.

Meaning (English): Passes on something you heard and asks for the listener's thoughts.
Watch out: Used for things heard from others, not witnessed firsthand. Frequently followed by a question or suggestion.

Meaning (English): Used to verify or confirm something you heard from someone else.
Watch out: Because you already heard about it, it is often paired with a welcoming tone or congratulations.

Meaning (English): Used to ask back in disbelief or surprise about something unexpected you just heard.
Watch out: Carries a stronger sense of surprise and disappointment than 「-다고요?」.

Meaning (English): Expresses that you are thinking about doing something, but have not made up your mind yet.
Form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ까」 / with final consonant + 「-을까」 + 「하다」
Watch out: Feels much less finalized than 「-(으)려고 하다」.

Meaning (English): A formal expression meaning 'in order to' or 'with the purpose of doing something'.
Watch out: Used in presentations and official documents. In spoken Korean, 「-(으)려고」 is more natural.

Meaning (English): Expresses that you were just about to do that very action.
Form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-려던」 / with final consonant + 「-으려던」 + 「참이다」
Watch out: Used when the other person's suggestion matches your exact plan. Pairs well with 「마침」.

Meaning (English): Indicates doing an action to serve dual purposes, killing two birds with one stone.
Form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 겸」 / with final consonant + 「-을 겸」 (Often used twice)
Watch out: Using it twice in a row sounds much more natural.
Example (Korean): 바람도 쐴 겸 산책도 할 겸 나왔어요.

Meaning (English): Expresses a firm personal resolution or reminds someone of what must rightfully be done.
Watch out: Used for both self-determination and scolding others. The latter carries a slightly reproaching tone.

Meaning (English): Indicates that something is worthwhile or worth doing.
Form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 만하다」 / with final consonant + 「-을 만하다」
Watch out: Used when making recommendations. 「먹을 만해요」 means it is acceptable, though not exceptionally delicious.

Meaning (English): Used to gently instruct or encourage someone to do something.
Watch out: Sounds stiffer than 「-(으)세요」, making it suitable for announcements and official instructions.

Meaning (English): Gently suggests a course of action, asking why you do not do it that way.
Watch out: The past form 「-지 그랬어요」 expresses regret that you did not do so.

Meaning (English): Modifies a noun to indicate a past repeated action or an unfinished state.
Watch out: While 「-(으)ㄴ」 marks a completed event, 「-던」 refers to repeated or discontinued habits.

Meaning (English): Shares a fact based on your own past direct experience or observation.
Watch out: Used only for things you directly witnessed yourself. Not used to describe your own subjective emotions.

Meaning (English): Shares what you directly observed in the past while leaving room for the listener to respond.
Watch out: Leaves more conversational room than 「-더라고요」, inviting the listener to continue speaking.

Meaning (English): Passive verbs indicating that an action is done to the subject. The affix varies by verb stem.
Watch out: Which affix attaches is fixed for each verb, so they must be memorized individually.

Meaning (English): Expresses a passive action without specifying who performed it.
Watch out: On adjectives, 「-아/어지다」 indicates change (e.g., 「따뜻해지다」); on verbs, it marks the passive voice.
Example (Korean): 이 책은 여러 나라 말로 번역됐어요.

Meaning (English): Indicates that a situation ended up that way regardless of your own intention.
Watch out: Gives the impression that it was not your own decision. Used to break personal news cautiously.

Meaning (English): Causative verbs indicating that the subject makes or lets someone else do an action.
Watch out: Many causative affixes overlap with passive forms. Distinguish them by identifying who performs the action.

Meaning (English): Indicates making, ordering, or allowing someone to perform an action.
Watch out: Used for verbs that lack single-word causative forms. Can be applied broadly.

Meaning (English): States an essential condition, meaning only if the first clause happens can the rest occur.
Watch out: Much stricter than 「-(으)면」. It emphasizes that without this condition, the result is impossible.

Meaning (English): Sets a condition meaning 'once/if that happens'. Followed by a request or suggestion.
Watch out: Different from causal 「-거든요」. This conditional form is followed by imperative or suggestive endings.

Meaning (English): Adds more information, meaning 'not only this, but also that'.
Form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 뿐만 아니라」 / with final consonant + 「-을 뿐만 아니라」 / Noun + 「뿐만 아니라」
Watch out: Both clauses must align in tone: positive points follow positive points, and negatives follow negatives.
Example (Korean): 값이 쌀 뿐만 아니라 맛도 좋아요.

Meaning (English): Indicates that an additional situation is compounded on top of the first one.
Form: Verb stem + 「-는 데다가」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 데다가」
Watch out: Conveys that situations overlap to intensify the result. Often paired with 「까지」 in the second clause.

Meaning (English): Even that one — and that is surprising.
Form: N + 조차 · usually followed by a negative
Watch out: For taking in even what you would not expect. A negative almost always follows.

Meaning (English): Gives an example, stating that just considering this single case proves the point.
Watch out: Means taking just one example among many is enough. Used when presenting evidence.

Meaning (English): On the way there or back.
Form: V + 는 길에 · attaches to going and coming verbs
Watch out: Only for verbs of going and coming. 「먹는 길에」 is wrong.

Meaning (English): Indicates that an action was interrupted or changed to another action midway.
Watch out: 「-다가」 indicates an interruption midway, whereas 「-았/었다가」 happens after full completion.

Meaning (English): Compares the degree of an action or state, meaning 'to the extent that'.
Form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 정도로」 / with final consonant + 「-을 정도로」
Watch out: Often used with vivid exaggeration to emphasize intensity.

Meaning (English): Indicates that the size or degree of something is roughly equivalent to the noun.
Watch out: Frequently used to compare physical sizes. While 「-보다」 marks difference, this marks similarity.

Meaning (English): Means 'as much as' or 'in proportion to' the extent of the action or state.
Form: Past: 「-(으)ㄴ 만큼」 / Present: 「-는 만큼」 / Future: 「-(으)ㄹ 만큼」 / Noun + 「만큼」
Watch out: While 「-(으)ㄹ 정도로」 tends to exaggerate, this denotes proportion—you get as much as you put in.

Meaning (English): Indicates that any person, item, or place is fine without restriction.
Watch out: In negative sentences, these change to 「아무도」, 「아무것도」, and 「아무 데도」.

Meaning (English): Expresses settling for an option as a second-best choice, even if not fully satisfied.
Form: Noun with final consonant + 「이나」 / without final consonant + 「나」
Watch out: Conveys picking an alternative out of lack of better options rather than picking your ideal choice.

Meaning (English): Not the best choice, but that one will do.
Form: 이라도 after a consonant · 라도 after a vowel
Watch out: Sounds more considerate than 「(이)나」. Use it when offering something.

Meaning (English): Indicates that choosing either option makes no difference.
Watch out: While 「-거나」 simply lists choices, this emphasizes complete indifference between either option.

Meaning (English): Indicates replacing one action or thing with another instead.
Form: Verb stem + 「-는 대신에」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 대신에」 / Noun + 「대신에」
Watch out: Also used for trade-offs or compensations, as in 「비싼 대신에 오래 써요」.

Meaning (English): Indicates that a certain amount of time has elapsed before an action takes place.
Watch out: 「동안」 refers to throughout that duration, while 「만에」 refers to after that duration has passed.

Meaning (English): Indicates completing an action and carrying that resulting state into the next action.
Watch out: Also used colloquially for causes: 「늦어 가지고 못 봤어요」. Do not use in formal writing.

Meaning (English): You did that, then switched to the opposite.
Watch out: It fits pairs that reverse each other: 「켜다 ↔ 끄다」, 「가다 ↔ 오다」.

Meaning (English): Clarifies sequential order, meaning doing the next action after completely finishing the first.
Watch out: Emphasizes the completion of the preceding action more clearly than 「-고」.

Meaning (English): Indicates realizing something new only after completing the action.
Watch out: The action comes first and the realization comes after. The phrase 「알고 보니」 is particularly common.
Example (Korean): 사고 보니 같은 게 집에 있었어요.

Meaning (English): You kept doing it, and this is how it turned out.
Watch out: 「-고 보니」 is after finishing once; this one is the result of repeating.

Meaning (English): Keep doing it and one day it will turn out that way.
Watch out: 「-다 보니」 already happened; this one is still ahead. Good for encouraging someone.

Meaning (English): Connects an observation you witnessed in the past with its resulting outcome.
Watch out: Used for other people's actions that you directly witnessed. For your own actions, use 「-았/었더니」.

Meaning (English): Expresses that doing a certain action resulted in a particular outcome or discovery.
Watch out: The first clause is what you did, and the second is the result. The subjects are opposite to 「-더니」.

Meaning (English): Warns that continuing to do an action will eventually lead to a bad result.
Watch out: Always followed by a negative outcome. Used to dissuade someone from doing something.

Meaning (English): Indicates that, all things considered, a situation is practically equivalent to something.
Form: Verb stem + 「-는 셈이다」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 셈이다」
Watch out: Means it is not strictly identical, but it can be considered practically the same.

Meaning (English): Indicates doing an action in advance and maintaining that resulting state.
Watch out: Almost identical to 「-아/어 두다」, but 「놓다」 is slightly more colloquial.

Meaning (English): Indicates doing an action in advance for future use or purpose.
Watch out: Carries a sense of keeping the state longer than 「놓다」, as in 「보관해 두다」.

Meaning (English): Indicates doing another action while maintaining the preceding state unchanged.
Form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄴ 채로」 / with final consonant + 「-은 채로」
Watch out: Usually used for situations where doing so is improper, as in 「불을 켠 채로 잤어요」.

Meaning (English): Means doing something exactly as it is, or immediately after an action occurs.
Form: Verb stem + 「-는 대로」 / Past tense + 「-(으)ㄴ 대로」 / Noun + 「대로」
Watch out: Also used to mean 'as soon as', as in 「도착하는 대로 연락할게요」.

Meaning (English): States that something leans toward a certain side rather than making a definitive claim.
Form: Verb stem + 「-는 편이다」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 편이다」
Watch out: Avoids blunt assertions, making it very common in self-introductions.
Example (Korean): 저는 매운 걸 잘 먹는 편이에요.

Meaning (English): Attaches to a noun to create an adjective meaning having that quality or impression.
Watch out: While 「답다」 means fitting the qualifications, 「스럽다」 means giving off that impression.

Meaning (English): Attaches to a noun to indicate being truly worthy of or matching its name.
Watch out: Mainly used for praise. 「어른답다」 means behaving up to the qualifications of an adult.

Meaning (English): Emphasizes the extreme degree of a state or action beyond description.
Watch out: Omitting the leading word 「얼마나」 changes the meaning. Always use them together.

Meaning (English): Expresses that there is no other choice or alternative but to do that action.
Form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 수밖에」 / with final consonant + 「-을 수밖에」 + 「없다」
Watch out: Means there is no other way. Used when making excuses or explaining inevitable circumstances.

Meaning (English): Expresses that something is only that one thing and nothing more.
Form: Verb/Adj stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 뿐」 / with final consonant + 「-을 뿐」 + 「이다」
Watch out: Used to speak modestly or to draw a clear line.

Meaning (English): That one, and nothing else, is the real thing.
Form: 이야말로 after a consonant · 야말로 after a vowel
Watch out: Suits writing and speeches. A little heavy for everyday talk.

Meaning (English): Indicates a purpose or goal, meaning 'so that' a certain state or action is achieved.
Watch out: Shorter and more casual than 「-도록」, making it much more frequent in spoken Korean.

Meaning (English): So that it turns out that way, or right up until then.
Watch out: It also means 'until', as in 「밤새도록」. More formal than 「-게」.
Example (Korean): 모두 들을 수 있도록 크게 말해 주세요.

Meaning (English): Indicates that an action was completed and then reversed to the opposite state.
Watch out: While 「-다가」 means interrupted midway, this occurs after full completion. A reverse action follows.

Meaning (English): Describes a noun by something that was true once, back then.
Watch out: 「-던」 is for what repeated or was left unfinished; this one finished once.

Meaning (English): Expresses completing an action entirely, accompanied by feelings of relief or regret.
Watch out: Carries two nuances: relief in 「끝내 버렸다」, or regret in 「잃어버렸다」.

Meaning (English): Expresses that a situation ended up happening in the end, with strong lingering regret.
Watch out: Carries deeper regret than 「-아/어 버리다」. Used when things did not turn out as desired.

Meaning (English): Expresses that doing or not doing the action makes no difference, so it is useless.
Form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-나 마나」 / with final consonant + 「-으나 마나」
Watch out: Used when the result is completely predictable. That obvious result follows in the next clause.
Example (Korean): 물어보나 마나 안 된다고 할 거예요.

Meaning (English): Expresses that even if you try doing the action, it will be useless or in vain.
Watch out: Followed by words indicating futility. More colloquial than 「-(으)나 마나」.

Meaning (English): Supposes that it were so. For things far from what is actually true.
Watch out: 「-(으)면」 is an ordinary condition; this one is an unlikely supposition.

Meaning (English): Expresses regret about a past situation, imagining what would have happened if things went differently.
Watch out: Used for past events that cannot be changed. Commonly followed by 「-았/었을 텐데」.
Example (Korean): 조금만 일찍 나왔더라면 안 늦었을 텐데요.

Meaning (English): Indicates that something almost happened, but ultimately did not occur in reality.
Form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ 뻔하다」 / with final consonant + 「-을 뻔하다」
Watch out: Used for things that did not actually occur. Always used in the past tense.

Meaning (English): Expresses personal regret, wishing that you had done a particular action.
Form: Verb stem without final consonant + 「-ㄹ걸」 / with final consonant + 「-을걸」 + 「그랬다」
Watch out: Shares a similar form with guessing 「-(으)ㄹ걸요」. Distinguish it by the ending 「그랬다」.

Meaning (English): Expresses regret that you should have done something, but failed to do so.
Watch out: Carries a heavier sense of admitting your own fault than 「-(으)ㄹ걸 그랬다」.

Meaning (English): Expresses a repeated habit or routine that you do from time to time.
Watch out: Use the past form 「-곤 했다」 for past habits: 「어릴 때 자주 놀곤 했어요」.

Meaning (English): Used to modestly deflect a compliment or apologize in a humble way.
Watch out: Used as a humble reply when receiving a compliment. Speak in a gentle tone.

Meaning (English): Indicates pretending to do or be something that is not true in reality.
Form: Verb stem + 「-는 척하다」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ 척하다」 / Past tense + 「-(으)ㄴ 척하다」
Watch out: While 「-는 것 같다」 is a guess, 「-는 척하다」 is an intentional pretense.

Meaning (English): Indicates that choosing the latter option is better than doing the former.
Watch out: Not used with the past tense marker 「-았/었-」.
Example (Korean): 이 값을 주고 사느니 차라리 만들어 쓰겠어요.

Meaning (English): Expresses choosing a better alternative since things have already ended up this way.
Watch out: Presupposes a predetermined situation. 「-느니」 compares two actions side by side.
Example (Korean): 늦게 갈 바에야 아예 가지 맙시다.

Meaning (English): Indicates that the outcome remains the same regardless of which option is chosen.
Watch out: Used by repeating the same word or pairing antonyms together.
Example (Korean): 비가 오건 눈이 오건 경기는 열립니다.

Meaning (English): Used to rephrase a statement, indicating that the latter expression is more accurate than the former.
Watch out: Ideal for softening and refining the other person's wording.

Meaning (English): A colloquial particle pointing to the person spoken to. Used among closer acquaintances than 「에게」.
Watch out: Used only in spoken Korean. Use 「에게」 in formal settings.

Meaning (English): Used to emphasize and reiterate what you already said.
Watch out: Repeats the same statement to express frustration or strong emphasis.

Meaning (English): Used to ask the listener for confirmation regarding a fact you heard.
Watch out: Since it asks for confirmation, pronounce it with a rising intonation at the end.

Meaning (English): A formal expression used to state the source of information.
Watch out: The following sentence naturally ends with a quoted citation form.
Example (Korean): 일기 예보에 의하면 내일 비가 온답니다.

Meaning (English): A written nominalizer that turns sentences into noun forms, commonly used in public notices and reports.
Watch out: Used in written public notices and reports. In spoken Korean, 「-는 것」 is more natural.

Meaning (English): Marks the process or the case of doing something.
Watch out: Unlike the connective 「-는데」, this one is written with a space.
Example (Korean): 집을 구하는 데 두 달이 걸렸어요.

Meaning (English): Used in formal contexts to refer to the preceding content and continue the statement.
Watch out: Mainly used in formal written documents.

Meaning (English): Used to state a cause in formal contexts. Frequently appears in news broadcasts and formal reports.
Watch out: Cannot be followed by imperative or suggestive sentences.

Meaning (English): Used when a chaotic or hectic situation leads to a bad outcome.
Watch out: Used only when the outcome is bad.
Example (Korean): 공사하는 통에 밤새 잠을 못 잤어요.

Meaning (English): Used in formal written Korean to state a cause or ground.
Watch out: Suited for formal written contexts like newspapers and academic papers.

Meaning (English): Indicates that the preceding content serves as a sufficient reason or ground for what follows.
Watch out: In practice, the form 「-(으)니만큼」 is used much more often.

Meaning (English): Indicates that since things have already turned out this way, one must naturally do the following action.
Watch out: Followed by expressions of obligation or strong determination.

Meaning (English): Indicates that no matter how much that may be the case, going that far is excessive.
Watch out: Typically paired with 「아무리」 in the first clause.

Meaning (English): Expresses that fortunately, taking that action prevented a serious disaster or trouble.
Watch out: Frequently followed by 「-(으)ㄹ 뻔했다」 in the next clause.
Example (Korean): 미리 예약했기에 망정이지 못 들어갈 뻔했어요.

Meaning (English): Used when someone did something under a plausible excuse but the result is displeasing.
Watch out: Conveys the speaker's displeasure or disapproval.

Meaning (English): Used to state a means or method of an action in formal contexts.
Watch out: Expresses a means, making it distinct from the causal form 「-(으)므로」.
Example (Korean): 서로 대화함으로써 갈등을 풀 수 있습니다.

Meaning (English): Used in written style to state a reason or ground for an action.
Watch out: The subject of the following clause is usually the speaker.

Meaning (English): Used in spoken Korean to give a reason. The subject of the first clause is usually not the speaker.
Watch out: Used in place of 「-기에」 in everyday spoken conversation.

Meaning (English): Even supposing that were so, the result does not change.
Watch out: It can also suppose something contrary to fact.

Meaning (English): A concessive expression meaning 'even if', stronger and more literary than 「-더라도」.
Watch out: Used formally in speeches and written texts.

Meaning (English): Means that doing so is useless, commonly used alongside a rhetorical question.
Watch out: Frequently followed by a rhetorical question.

Meaning (English): Indicates that even if the first condition is accepted, one will firmly uphold the following principle.
Watch out: The first clause sets a bad condition, while the second shows a resolute attitude.

Meaning (English): Used to assume and accept something as true, even if it is not actually the case.
Watch out: Frequently used in the form 「-다 치더라도」.

Meaning (English): Indicates considering or treating something as such, even though it is not true in reality.
Watch out: Used when making up your mind while regarding a situation differently from reality.

Meaning (English): Emphasizes that the second action occurs immediately as soon as the first action finishes.
Watch out: The two actions happen so quickly they feel almost simultaneous.

Meaning (English): A written expression indicating that the second action immediately follows the first.
Watch out: Cannot be used with imperative or suggestive endings.

Meaning (English): Means 'as long as' or 'while that condition is maintained'.
Watch out: Refers to the duration during which a condition remains true.
Example (Korean): 내가 아는 한 그런 규정은 없습니다.

Meaning (English): Indicates that whenever you try to do an action, an interruption always gets in the way.
Watch out: Used for recurring, frustrating interruptions.

Meaning (English): A written expression meaning 'if you keep on doing that action'.
Watch out: Being a literary form, it fits words of personal resolution or comfort.

Meaning (English): Indicates that the outcome depends entirely on that factor.
Watch out: Naturally pairs with question words in the clause.

Meaning (English): Indicates that the outcome changes depending on how one does or perceives it.
Watch out: Frequently used like a short proverb or maxim.

Category: Expressing Doing Things Separately and Together
Meaning (English): Indicates that each item has its own distinct usefulness or value respectively.
Watch out: Repeated twice in the same form to create a contrast.
Example (Korean): 이건 이것대로 저건 저것대로 쓸모가 있어요.

Category: Expressing Doing Things Separately and Together
Meaning (English): Indicates taking the opportunity of doing one action to do another at the same time.
Watch out: Used when adding a secondary action to the main intended task.

Meaning (English): A written expression showing regret that the result fell short of expectations despite the preceding effort.
Watch out: A literary ending carrying feelings of regret and disappointment.

Meaning (English): Indicates acting in an opposite or contradictory way even after doing that action.
Watch out: The subject must be identical in both the preceding and following clauses.

Meaning (English): A formal expression meaning 'in spite of' or 'despite that'.
Watch out: Well suited for formal written texts and presentations.

Meaning (English): Used to make a comparison, meaning 'just as' or 'as if'.
Watch out: Frequently used in proverbs and figurative expressions.

Meaning (English): Indicates that an action is practically equivalent to doing that, almost to the point of being true.
Watch out: Means it is not literally the case, but very close to it.

Meaning (English): Indicates that not only the first statement is true, but the following is even more so.
Watch out: Both clauses must align in the same positive or negative direction.

Meaning (English): Far from what you expected — the opposite happened instead.
Watch out: A negative follows.

Meaning (English): Adds further information, meaning 'not only that, but also...'.
Watch out: Group positive traits together with positives, and negatives with negatives.

Meaning (English): Used to grant permission for the first action while attaching a specific condition.
Watch out: Fits rules, guidelines, and formal instructions.

Meaning (English): Even the last one left is included.
Watch out: Usually for a situation you regret.

Meaning (English): Used to list several items by putting the primary or representative one first.
Watch out: Introduces a list by placing the representative example at the front.

Meaning (English): Expresses negative disapproval toward someone repeatedly performing an excessive action.
Watch out: Due to its negative nuance, do not use it when speaking about elders or superiors.

Meaning (English): Indicates that something happens frequently, used mostly for bad or undesirable events.
Watch out: Used to describe bad habits or recurring negative occurrences.

Meaning (English): Indicates doing an action half-heartedly or barely doing it at all.
Form: Verb stem + 「-는 둥 마는 둥 하다」
Watch out: Expresses an insincere or careless attitude.
Example (Korean): 밥을 먹는 둥 마는 둥 하고 나갔다.

Meaning (English): A formal written expression meaning 'to the extent that' or 'so much that'.
Watch out: Has the same meaning as 「-(으)리만큼」.

Meaning (English): Indicates reaching an extreme point where one can no longer endure, leading to an outcome.
Watch out: Also used when an extreme degree causes a change into a different state.

Meaning (English): Used when intending to do one action unexpectedly resulted in a different, mistaken outcome.
Watch out: Used only when the outcome differs from what was intended.

Meaning (English): Indicates intending to do something but giving it up midway.
Watch out: Used when you changed your mind and decided not to do the action.

Meaning (English): Indicates that something looked like it was about to happen and ended up actually occurring.
Watch out: Used in situations where an initial expectation turns out to be correct.

Meaning (English): Indicates acting in a manner that makes it appear as though something is true.
Watch out: Placed directly before an action to describe how it is performed.

Meaning (English): Means 'as if saying that', showing something through facial expressions or actions.
Watch out: Used when expressing a thought through looks or gestures instead of spoken words.

Meaning (English): Used to make a gentle, soft guess that something seems to be the case.
Watch out: Softer and more literary than 「-는 것 같다」.

Meaning (English): Used when you are entirely certain that an obvious outcome will happen.
Watch out: Because it expresses confident certainty, it is frequently used for negative outcomes.
Example (Korean): 지금 가 봤자 문 닫았을 게 뻔해요.

Meaning (English): Indicates that a situation or feeling is fully understandable and natural.
Watch out: Used when showing empathy and understanding toward another person's feelings.

Meaning (English): Strongly denies something, stating there is absolutely no reason or possibility for it.
Watch out: Used for strong denial or firm conviction.

Meaning (English): Means that it is very easy or likely to end up in a certain state, usually a negative one.
Watch out: Frequently used when giving advice or warnings.

Meaning (English): Expresses that it is natural and inevitable for something to happen that way.
Watch out: Also written and used as 「-게 마련이다」.

Meaning (English): Used to state a universal principle or natural law of the world.
Watch out: Used like a proverb or maxim to state how things naturally work.

Meaning (English): Indicates that while one case exists, another contrasting or different case also occurs.
Form: Verb stem + 「-는가 하면」 / Adj stem + 「-(으)ㄴ가 하면」
Watch out: Places two different cases side by side.

Meaning (English): Expresses that there is a lot of talk and gossip about this and that.
Watch out: Used by pairing opposing or contrasting words together.

Meaning (English): Lists multiple tasks to vividly describe being extremely busy doing this and that.
Watch out: Vividly lists tasks to emphasize a hectic situation.

Meaning (English): Used to list multiple items together, meaning 'this, that, and more'.
Watch out: Lists multiple things all at once.

Meaning (English): Indicates that an outcome was reached after a long period of struggle or effort.
Watch out: Preceded by a process that took a long time and significant effort.

Meaning (English): Expresses finally accomplishing a difficult task through hard work and persistence.
Watch out: Used for achievements attained after great effort.

Meaning (English): Indicates that an emotion or state became so extreme that it resulted in a certain outcome.
Watch out: Expresses an outcome caused by an excessive degree in the first clause.

Meaning (English): Used to report and recall something you directly observed or experienced in the past.
Watch out: Used only for things seen firsthand; use 「-대요」 for things heard from others.

Meaning (English): Means in the middle of or while such an ongoing situation continues.
Watch out: Frequently appears in news broadcasts and media reports.

Meaning (English): Means 'now that things have reached this point', referring to a critical situation.
Watch out: Used in urgent, awkward, or difficult situations.

Meaning (English): Indicates that there is no exception within that category, or means 'considering that'.
Watch out: When used as 「치고는」, it conveys that something is unexpected for that category.

Meaning (English): Indicates that as the first change occurs, the following situation also changes accordingly.
Watch out: Suited for texts explaining data, trends, and reports.
Example (Korean): 기온이 높아짐에 따라 전력 사용이 늘었다.

Meaning (English): Means that something is extraordinary, indicating an extreme degree.
Watch out: Must always end in a negative grammatical form.

Meaning (English): Means that a quality is beyond description, being as extreme as can be.
Watch out: Used for high praise or strong admiration.

Meaning (English): Expresses that even if you desperately want or try to do an action, you cannot do it at all.
Form: Verb stem + 「-(으)려야」 + Verb stem + 「-(으)ㄹ 수가 없다」
Watch out: Repeats the same verb stem twice.
Example (Korean): 그날 일은 잊으려야 잊을 수가 없어요.

Meaning (English): An archaic, respectful speech style preserved in public notices and historical texts.
Watch out: Seen in historical public notices, subtitles, and traditional stories.

Meaning (English): A speech style used to address people of lower status with a certain degree of respect.
Watch out: Traditionally used by teachers to students or fathers-in-law to sons-in-law.

Meaning (English): Written connecting endings used for expressing reason, contrast, and listing.
Watch out: In spoken Korean, 「-니까, -지만, -고」 are more natural.

Meaning (English): Deals with the structural forms of passive and causative verbs.
Watch out: Even for the same verb stem, the meaning changes depending on the attached affix.

Meaning (English): Advanced Korean grammatical expressions useful to recognize in literary texts.
Watch out: Frequently encountered in literary and formal written works.
